theme: Praise the name of the LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 135. It is a hymn of praise that celebrates the LORD’s greatness over the idols of the nations. Notice how it echoes Daniel’s chapters: the God of Israel against the gods of Babylon.
settingTheScene: Psalm 135 is a hymn built from other Scripture. It quotes Exodus, Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and other psalms. It was sung after the exile as the community recalled what God had done. It comes at the right place in this unit, after the stories of Daniel, where the living God confronts idols and kings. The psalm mocks idols and praises God for his choice of Israel. It will appear again later in the plan.
observation: “Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD” (v. 1).
“For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods” (v. 5).
“Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps” (v. 6).
“He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast” (v. 8).
“Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages” (v. 13).
“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (v. 15).
“They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see” (vv. 16-17).
“Those who make them become like them, so do all who trust in them” (v. 18).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a call to praise and quickly gives reasons: the LORD is good, he chose Jacob, and he is great. The key statement is in verse 6: “Whatever the LORD pleases, he does.” This is God’s sovereignty. Unlike the idols, he acts, in the heavens and on earth. He makes clouds rise, lightning flash, and wind come from his storehouses. In history, he struck down the firstborn of Egypt and defeated kings such as Sihon and Og. He gave their land as a heritage to Israel.

The psalm then contrasts God with idols. The idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear, and there is no breath in their mouths. The list is almost comical, and it is exactly the argument Isaiah and Jeremiah made. And the psalm ends with the most striking line: “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.” We become like what we worship. People who worship dead things become dead. They lose sight, hearing, and speech. Those who worship the living God become alive.

The final section widens the call to praise. The house of Israel, the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, and all who fear the LORD are summoned to bless him. And the last line is: “Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!”

For the exiles, who saw the grandeur of Babylon’s temples and idols, this was an important reminder. The gods of the empire were silent and powerless. The God of Israel, who seemed to be defeated, was alive and in control. The statue of Daniel 2 and the image of Daniel 3 were nothing before him.
connection: Acts 14:15-17 and 17:24-29 use this argument to preach to pagans. 1 Corinthians 8:4-6 says there is no God but one. Romans 1:22-23 says people who exchange the glory of God for images become fools. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says that beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image. 1 Peter 2:9 calls the church a chosen race, God’s own possession, to proclaim his excellencies. Revelation 4:11 praises the worthy Lord and God.
application:
Ask what you tend to worship that cannot speak, see, or hear. What are you becoming like?

Use this psalm as a call to praise. Name what the LORD has done as a list in your own words.

Say verse 6 as a statement of trust: “Whatever the LORD pleases, he does.”
prayerPrompts: Praise God as great above all gods.
Confess any idol of silver and gold, literal or modern.
Thank him for what he pleases to do.
